- **POLY-nf.** No needs. *Note:* Added 2026-11-07: QUESTIONS Q10 was withdrawn as decided by the no-thresholds rule, since a grade that changes when an expansion outgrows its text is a change of behavior at a size. This row replaces sec:optimizer's no-growth rule (zed, same day) and takes over MOD-residue's normal form, refusal measurement and `^` lowering, so that rung 3 (L3.9, level 22) does not wait for level 49. Complexity tradeoff: a product of s sums of t terms has up to t^s monomials, and squaring a sum of k terms forms (k + 1)^2 products for 2k + 1 monomials, so multiplication must be O(n log n) in the normal cases (Kronecker substitution to one variable and FFT multiplication where the product is dense; BIGINT-fast-mul's code may serve), measured under the Q3 procedure; a quadratic site needs the author's approval. Measure the normal forms of every product in the corpus's obligations before fixing any refused shape; each refused shape is structural and its site carries a `// Complexity tradeoff:` comment. Check first whether `^` with a literal exponent reaches the checker as a product, and lower it to one here if not. *Test:* `law diffSquares(x: int, y: int) = (x + y) * (x - y) == x * x - y * y;` is proved; `(a + b) * (c + d) * (e + f)` equal to its eight written monomials is proved; `law sumSquare(x: int) = (1 + x + x ^ 2 + x ^ 3) ^ 2 == (1 + x) ^ 2 * (1 + x ^ 2) ^ 2;` is proved (16 products, 7 monomials); `law wrong(x: int, y: int) = (x + y) * (x + y) == x * x + y * y;` is refuted with `x = 1, y = 1` printed; a false identity of a refused shape is refuted at a point and a true one is rejected with the refusal error; the points are the same on every run and in batch and single-file checking; `(1 + x + ... + x ^ k) ^ 2` at k and 8k, and products of n and 8n monomials, grow as n log n.
- **POLY-nf-power.** Needs POLY-nf (the module it changes). *Note:* Added 2026-11-12 (the author asked to look at the count of a power). The count `n * sums(a)` refused `(x + y) ^ 4`, which has 5 monomials; a power of a base of at most T monomials has at most C(T + n − 1, T − 1) ≤ (n + 1)^(T − 1), the bound of a product of T − 1 sums of n + 1 terms, so it counts the fewer of the two. Measured with the old count bypassed, instructions at k and 8k: `(x + y) ^ k` against its expansion, k = 64, 50.5 times before and 12.9 after the gcd step; `(x + y + z) ^ k`, k = 16, 1491 before and 93.8 after, for 512 times the output bits. Found the flaw of POLY-nf-power-value (QUESTIONS A98) and the leftover cost of POLY-nf-sparse-product. *Test:* `l03_09_egraph::refusal::a_power_of_a_sum_counts_its_terms`, `scaling::a_power_of_a_sum_of_two_names` (k = 500, order 2), `poly::tests::refused_shapes`, `the_dense_and_sparse_products_agree`; negative control, run once: main's poly.rs refuses the scaling test.
- **POLY-nf-power-value.** Needs POLY-nf-power (the count it extends), and the answer to QUESTIONS A98 (ledger: waiting on QUESTIONS-answered). *Note:* Added 2026-11-12 by POLY-nf-power, which reproduced it: `(1 + x) ^ k == (1 + x) ^ (k / 2) * (1 + x) ^ (k / 2)` is proved in 0.37 s at k = 4096 and 13.8 s, 5.39 GB allocated, 1.16 GB resident, at k = 32768, Θ(k²); k = 65536, 2^20, 2^24 and 2^32 run past 60 s. The hard rule of sec:plan bars an algorithm exponential in the size of its input, and the exponent's digits are its size. The fast path is decided by the standing rule that simple cases get fast paths and needs no answer. Feeds S.3-cost-types (the kernel's scaling join), where its tests must pass. *Test:* the example of A98 proved in O(L log n); under the answer chosen, `(x + y) ^ 1048576 == (y + x) ^ 1048576` proved by the fast path, and an identity that needs the expansion of such a power (`(1 + x) ^ 1048576 - (1 - x) ^ 1048576 == 0`, false) refuted at a point; a scaling test of the exponent's digits at n and 8n. *Answered 2026-11-12 (author, A98):* answer A, with the size measured as the term, not the source text: "defined by non-whitespace chars, or better, the length in bits of the operands combined in some reasonable way -- reason about this (just taking the cube of the source length is very ad hoc)". Orchestrator reading: n = the identity's size as a term (one per operator and name, plus the bit length of every integer literal, exponents included; whitespace, comments, name length and literal spelling do not count); W = an upper bound on the bit operations of the expansion, read from the shape in one pass (a sum adds monomial counts; a product of a and b costs m_a * m_b coefficient products at the cost of their bit lengths; a power by its squarings); expand iff W <= K(n), K(n) = W of the most expensive product of three sums of total size n, the most the present four-sum refusal admits, so the degree is the one already accepted and no constant is chosen; past it, the refusal "Cannot expand" with its menu and a sec:diagnostics row. This one rule replaces the count of sums (a product of four one-letter sums is then accepted). Before merge: measure that W tracks time and bytes over the POLY-nf families and the corpus obligations (W at n and 8n against measured cost), and send the bound to cross-review if it does not. The fast path for powers of one base is built under every answer. *Progress 2026-11-12 (POLY-nf-power-value, impl 1):* the fast path is built and merged: products of powers of the same factors are compared with each factor expanded once (`Decision::factored`), so A98 `split` at 2^32 and `(x + y) ^ 1048576 == (y + x) ^ 1048576` are proved, scaling of the exponent digits 1.1 times from 16 to 128 bits. The size rule is not built: W measured against instructions does not track the kernel within a constant factor (2003 down to 6.6 instructions per unit of W across the POLY-nf families, a 20-fold fall from n to 8n on `(x + y) ^ k`), and K(n) = q^3 + 2.5q^2 + 1.5q - 2 at s = 3q terms, about ((n + 1)/6)^3, refuses exponent 1000 and `a + c == c + a`; open for cross-review (CD first, then Sol, Opus, Gemini) with the prototype /home/luke/Work/wt/cd-xr/POLY-nf-power-value-W-prototype.diff and COMPLEXITY.md POLY-nf-power-value. Still open here: A98 `product` at 2^32, and `(a+b)(c+d)(e+f)(g+h)` accepted.
- **POLY-nf-sparse-product.** Needs POLY-nf-power (the product it changes). *Note:* Added 2026-11-12 by POLY-nf-power: the gcd step removes the empty indices of homogeneous sums, but `((x + y) ^ k + x) ^ 2` still costs 103 times the instructions at k = 64 to 512 and 300 times at k = 256 to 2048, for 64 times the output. Prior art: Arnold and Roche, "Output-sensitive algorithms for sumset and sparse polynomial multiplication" (ISSAC 2015, arXiv 1501.05296), softly linear in the input, the output and the sumset of the supports; it is randomized, so its choices must be drawn from content addresses and its product checked, so that the result is the same on every run. Feeds S.3-cost-types. *Test:* `((x + y) ^ k + x) ^ 2` at k and 8k within the n log n limit, with the dense and sparse products as negative controls. *Done:* 2026-11-12, the support product (`Poly::support_mul`, `sumset`, `coefficients`), tried first when its cost formula is below the cheaper of the dense and sparse products; its primes are drawn from a digest of the sides' indices and every index and coefficient is taken only from a slot proved to hold it alone, so the product is exact on every input and the work the same on every run. `l03_09_egraph::bench::scaling::the_square_of_a_power_of_a_sum_beside_one_name` at k = 256 and 2048: 22.9 times the instructions and 21.4 times the bytes for 64 times the output (limit 96.8); negative controls: main's choice 140.6 times the bytes, the dense and the sparse product alone past 60 s (COMPLEXITY POLY-nf-sparse-product).

- **ERRS-precise.** No open needs (L1.18 and L1.27 are done). *Note:* DESIGN.md sec:failure merges equal failures into one and makes a singleton the atom itself, but the checker added `#errs(..)` whenever two operands could fail, so `x + y` of two `int | #notFound` printed `int | #errs(..) | #notFound` though no value of that type is ever `#errs`. `ty::merges` decides in O(n), by comparing each operand's failures with the first, at `passed` and `outside_of`; a payload atom such as `#syntaxError(int)` counts as several failures. The merged failure's static type is `#errs(E ->? E)`, `E` the union of the operands' loose failures with the members of an operand's own `#errs` flattened in, so a chain holds one `#errs` and never a nested one; it prints with `E` written out and parses back to the same type (`{…}` in a type holds literals only, sec:grammar `SetType`, so DESIGN's `#errs({E})` was not type syntax; the spec branch writes `#errs(E ->? E)` at its three type uses). An operand whose `#errs` members are not known makes the merge's members unknown, `#errs(..)`; `outside_of` and `unnamed_of` still add `#errs(..)`, which is sound but wider. Building `E` along a chain made `Atoms::zip` in the kernel walk the whole smaller map at each step, O(n²) for n different failures; it now also walks the diff of the two maps, which skips the nodes they share (COMPLEXITY.md F101). allOk (DESIGN.md:513) is not part of this item; row L3.2 builds it, as DESIGN step L3.2 (DESIGN.md:2015) and the layer table (DESIGN.md:4091) say; the orchestrator's assignment of 2026-11-05 to L2.7 was wrong. (On 2026-11-07 the author removed allOk; steps L2.6b, L3.2b and L6.5d replace it.) Feeds L2.7.

- **PRODUCT-nested-chain.** Needs ST-arms-quad, ST-formula-share, ST-ladder, F70-rerun (the measured cause, added 2026-11-05). *Option (a), 2026-11-05, from the study of Adams et al. 2011 (wt/study-linearlog/REPORT.md, candidate B; their section 3.2 reads each node once, bottom up) as fitted to F70-rerun's measurement (COMPLEXITY F70):* `arms` itself does little here. The outer test `(if … ) == 1` is one atom, and `preimage::linear` turns the whole nest into one relation, a nest of d disjunctions linked through `n`. `presburger::project_parts` then calls `settle_as_sets` once per level, about d^2 disjuncts are solved in all, and each solve takes the whole linked base (`Linked::around`, about 0.65d rows): d^3. The fix keeps each inner `if` as a summary computed once, bottom up: for each outcome of its test, the product of its value (the interval set of `n` on that arm and the arm's linear value) and the scope on that outcome. The preimage of the level above reads the summary in place of the inner relation, so each level costs O(1) summaries and the nest O(d). The same summary serves `Scope::cases` where an inner `if` is a node of the test's `Tree`. Wherever a summary widens a hull that the exact projection keeps, put a `// Complexity tradeoff:` comment at that site. The comment names the inputs whose hull widens, says why (the exact projection settles every level against the whole linked base, d^3), names the trigger (an `if` nested inside a compared value), and names this row's test and COMPLEXITY F70. On the measured family each summary is exact and of constant size (true arm `n` in `[1..=1]` with value `n`, false arm `n` in `[..=0, 2..]` with value `2n`), so option (a) reaches O(d); a nest whose arms' interval sets grow with depth makes the summaries grow too, and the test at d and 8d must then still hold. *Considered and not adopted (F70-rerun merge check, 2026-11-05):* (b) give each disjunct only the base rows linked to its own atoms by a union-find over shared atoms. `Linked` is already that union-find, and every row of this nest mentions `n`; counters showed about one group per solve and 97 to 99% of the base rows handed over, so (b) removes nothing, score 0 of 10. (c) An incremental solve against a base kept solved: the d^2 solves remain, so O(d^2) at best, score 2 of 10. Option (a), O(d) on this family, score 8 of 10 (minus for the hulls it may widen elsewhere). *Note:* Ledger queued with feeds L1.40, T12 and no plan row, so plan_dag.md:31-32's rule failed until this row. COMPLEXITY F70 says not fixed, rerun 2026-11-05 by F70-rerun: Θ(d^3). ST-arms-quad fixed another cost on deep conditions. The earlier figure, about d^2.4 (76 MB at d = 16 to 1.2 GB at d = 48), came from small d. *Test:* The `chain` input of tests/steps/l01_39_reduced_product/follow.rs:84 at d and 8d within 24x in time and bytes; today's code is the negative control; arms equal. Also: Same answers as now on the corpus and random inputs. Scaling: n and 8n within 24x. Corner: depth 48. Negative control, run once and never committed: the old arms must exceed 24x. *Changed 2026-11-07 (DAG-fanin):* needs implied by a longer path dropped, each reason above still holding through the path named: ST-arms-quad (via ST-ladder). *Needs now:* ST-ladder, ST-formula-share, F70-rerun.

Unobservable to programs, so placing it before S.1 costs order only. *Integer ranges (author, 2026-11-09):* a union of one or more atoms with an integer domain that does not fill its word stores the atoms in unused values of the word instead of a separate tag, so the value is not a pair (number, atom). The atoms take the bit patterns of -1, -2, and so on down, the old convention: in a signed word these are -1 and -2, in an unsigned word its largest values (255 and 254 in `u8`). Where the domain holds those patterns (`int[-5..<100]`), the atoms take the values just past the domain's other end. The test for an atom is then one comparison with the domain's bound, and a `match` over the atoms is one jump table. Where the word has fewer unused values than atoms, a separate tag is kept, with a `// Complexity tradeoff:` comment if a wider word was weighed. *Test:* `int[0..=254] | #none` in a narrow column is one byte; `f64 | #none` is eight; `int[0..<100] | #unknown | #bad` is one byte, with `#unknown` and `#bad` stored as 255 and 254 in `u8`, and as -1 and -2 in `i8` when the domain is `int[0..<100]` in a signed column; `int[-5..<100] | #unknown | #bad` uses 100 and 101; `int[0..=255] | #none` keeps a tag. Differential test: every value and atom round-trips through the packed form. Corner cases: no spare value left; foreign and grammar formats excluded. Scaling: layout choice at n and 8n members within 24x. Negative control, run once and never committed: make the spare value collide with a real value and require the differential test to fail. Recommended form with no grammar change: a run option mapping a generation variable's keypath to a function in the edited source, the option kept in the replay record, stated in a "Where this document does not say" paragraph; `@migrate` was weighed and costs a word for nothing the test checks. This overrides the correction at pass2:156 that said no such row is needed; that reviewer looked at the L34.1 and L32.2 order, not at the placement rule. *Test:* DESIGN:2707 moves here, run from recorded inputs and a recorded edit list with no editor: under replay each frame equals a fresh run of the edited program on the recorded inputs; under continue each frame equals a fresh run started from the kept, migrated and restarted frames. *Rewritten 2026-11-19 (SPEC-c15-answer, author's answer to C15, study docs/edit-state-reuse-study.md):* an edit that changes a frame type with no migration is no longer rejected; the variable restarts from its `initial` value with every generation variable that reads it, and the report names them; a removed variable is dropped and named without a migration; a rename is a removal and an addition unless `--migrate new=old` names it; `--migrate new=f`, `--migrate new=f(old, ...)` and `--migrate new=old` are the run option's three forms, recorded with the edit; a migration of the wrong type is rejected naming the variable; a migration that fails at run time rejects the whole edit and the run goes on with the old program. Unchanged nodes keep their values by upstream hash (equal hash confirmed by a check of the node's own term and its inputs' matches), adopting or repacking the old storage; under replay outputs before the edit's wave are reported, not written again. The full list of tests is step L34.1's, run here at the command line. A recording with edits replays bit-exactly, and the same recording with its edit waves removed, given the edited program, is refused. Negative controls, run once and not committed: treat an edit as a fresh program with no address check, and the refusal case fails; skip the structural check of an upstream-hash match and force two hashes equal, and the reuse test reports a wrong value. Corner cases: an edit that changes no value, two edits in one wave, an edit before the first wave, a variable moved to another keypath (a removal and an addition), a reordered recursive group (recomputed, equal values), a loop whose guard changed (its kept instances reused, the new ones computed). Run options hashed into the upstream hash: none beyond the term, since no run option changes a value outside it (decided 2026-11-19, EDIT-reuse-open-points; DESIGN sec:incremental lists them): `build.options` and `build.target` are literals after resolution, so a node reading one has a different hash under different options (tested in step L2.8d by the replay of a record under other options). A migration's parameter may be any type of the edited source that the old frame type is a subtype of (same decision). Scaling: replay of n and 8n recorded waves with one edit, the work per wave stopping at the cutoff; applying one edit to programs of n and 8n nodes and to runs of n and 8n frame instances; each within the limit of the scaling test (T(8n)/T(n) < 10.5). *Changed 2026-11-07 (DAG-fanin):* needs implied by a longer path dropped, each reason above still holding through the path named: L7.3 (via MEMO-edit), L7.6 (via MEMO-edit), L7.13 (via MEMO-edit). *Needs now:* MEMO-edit. *Added in batch 105:* L1.19d, the offline replay of a recording against an edited program, which this row extends (DESIGN step L1.19d).

The paper proves (p7, Fig. 10) that an analysis giving each expression a full environment, and one for each outcome of a test, is O(n²). Today the checker narrows only the names a test mentions and restores them (`check/mod.rs`), and a join of two `Scope`s walks only what the arms changed (`store/product.rs`, `Scope::join`); L1.40b must keep that shape when the checker reads the store. The paper's own O(n log n) method (section 4) does not carry over, since relations between names break its guard property and the lattices have unbounded height. Feeds L1.40b. *Test:* k names and d nested tests, each test mentioning one name, at k = d; bytes and instructions at n and 8n within 24x, with the inputs built before timing. Negative control, run once and not committed: a version that copies the whole environment at each test must exceed 24x.

After the author's follow-up (byte order marks, no-break spaces and other characters used in composition), the set is Default_Ignorable_Code_Point plus the three characters of XID_Start or XID_Continue whose glyph is blank but which lack that property, U+13441 and U+13442 (Egyptian hieroglyph blanks) and U+16FE4 (Khitan small script filler); outside names `Space` already admits only U+0020, tab and the line breaks. The messages name by its code point every character of the general categories Cc, Cf, Zs, Zl, Zp, Co, Cs and Cn, every White_Space character, every character of no width and every character a name may not hold. The set is the Unicode property Default_Ignorable_Code_Point, wider than the joiners A97 asked about; the Hangul fillers are XID_Start letters, so the rule covers a name's first character. The grammar engine runs `XID_START` and `XID_CONTINUE` as code (crates/zedc-syntax/src/parse/engine.rs), so the PEG class, the engine and the lexer change together. *Test:* each Default_Ignorable character inside a name and at its start is an error at its span with the code-point message; each is accepted in a comment and in string text; `a_zero_width_joiner_or_non_joiner_inside_a_name_is_part_of_it` becomes a test of the error; a check that the table of excluded characters equals the property in the Unicode data the lexer's other tables use.
